paras: The threatened lynching of Peter Moore took place at Hempstead, Texas, in November 1880, after Moore, a Black man, was accused of shooting and killing City Marshal J. H. Adams. Threats of hanging led a deputy sheriff to move Moore to the jail at Brenham for safekeeping, and a Minnesota paper reported that a vigilance committee had formed and his lynching was expected. No attack on Moore was reported; he was tried at Hempstead in April 1881 and sentenced to seven years for second-degree murder.

Adams, described as Hempstead's assistant city marshal or city marshal, was shot on Saturday, November 6, 1880, at night according to the Dallas Daily Herald. The Herald said Moore shot him because Adams had tried to arrest him, and the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman said the marshal was shot in the head. Adams died and was buried at Hempstead, according to a state-news column in the Brenham Weekly Banner.

According to the Brenham Weekly Banner, "threats of hauging were liberally indulged in at Hempstead" after the shooting. On the following Tuesday, Deputy Sheriff Chambers and two assistants brought Moore by the Central train from Hempstead and placed him in the Brenham jail for safekeeping. The same paper's state column said a vigilance committee was rumored to have been organized against Moore, while the St. Paul Daily Globe reported on November 18 that a committee "has been organized, and the lynching of Moore is looked for." None of the papers reports a crowd gathering or any attempt to take Moore from the jail.

Moore went on trial at Hempstead on April 12, 1881, for the murder of Adams and pleaded not guilty, with District Attorney Hanny prosecuting and H. M. Browne for the defense. Three venires of 130 men were exhausted that day to seat eight jurors, six Black and two white, many of "our best citizens" having disqualified themselves for opinions or prejudices while "very few colored jurors" excused themselves. On April 14 the jury, after fourteen hours, found Moore guilty of murder in the second degree and gave him seven years in the penitentiary.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers, most of it in short items in Texas state-news columns. The Brenham Weekly Banner treated the accusation as settled, calling Moore "the negro who murdered city marshal Adams" and "a bad negro," and reported the hanging threats without comment. The Austin and Dallas papers added that he had earlier served a sentence for killing "another white man," five years by their count against the Banner's two.

Outside Texas the story ran only as fragments: the New-York Tribune and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle carried a garbled Galveston wire, a Vermont weekly placed Adams in Galveston, and the St. Paul Daily Globe printed the one report of an expected lynching. The Dallas Herald covered the trial through a Hempstead correspondent, who called the case "a sad commentary upon our jury system," and its weekly edition reprinted both dispatches.

The first wire report, dated Hempstead, November 7, said that Adams had "shot and fatally wounded Peter Moore." Every later account named Moore as the shooter and Adams as the dead man, and Moore's jailing and his trial for Adams's murder show that he survived, so the first wire appears to have reversed the two names.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Peter Moore
bases: Threats of hanging at Hempstead led officers to move Moore to the Brenham jail, and a Minnesota brief reported a vigilance committee and an expected lynching (A6, A9); no attack on Moore was reported.

The threatened hanging was a response to Moore's alleged killing of the marshal, but no one killed him: he was jailed at Brenham, tried at Hempstead in April 1881 and sentenced to seven years (A6, A13, A16). This was a threatened lynching only.

The local Brenham Weekly Banner reports the hanging threats and the transfer for safekeeping, and the Daily Globe separately reports a vigilance committee and an expected lynching (A6, A9); the Banner's own state column calls the committee a rumor (A4).

framing.detail: The Brenham Weekly Banner called Moore 'the negro who murdered city marshal Adams' and 'a bad negro' while reporting the threats without criticism.
The Austin and Dallas papers ran the case as one-line state news ('Another murder at Heupstead'), stressing Moore's race and a prior term for killing 'another white man'.
The Daily Globe's 'Globelets' column reported the committee and that 'the lynching of Moore is looked for' without comment.
The Dallas Herald's April trial dispatch noted that six of eight jurors were Black and called the case 'a sad commentary upon our jury system.'

versions.value: Adams shot and fatally wounded Moore (November 7 Hempstead wire).

conflicts.note: The later Texas reports, the jailing of Moore, and his April 1881 trial for Adams's murder show Moore survived; the early wire appears to have reversed the names. Whether Moore was wounded is not reported.
The Brenham column is local but badly garbled; the Globe brief is distant and secondhand.
